topics.title: Lists, Slicing and Sorting
topics.summary: Ordered, mutable sequences with indexing, slicing, common methods and sorting.
topics.description:
A `list` is an ordered, **mutable** collection that can hold any mix of types. It is the most-used container in Python.

### Core operations
- Index: `a[0]`, `a[-1]` (last).
- Add: `append(x)`, `extend(iterable)`, `insert(i, x)`.
- Remove: `pop()`, `pop(i)`, `remove(x)`, `del a[i]`, `clear()`.
- Info: `len(a)`, `x in a`, `a.index(x)`, `a.count(x)`.

### Slicing
`a[start:stop:step]` returns a **new list**; `stop` is excluded and every part is optional. `a[::-1]` reverses, `a[:3]` takes the first three, `a[1::2]` takes every second item starting at index 1. Slicing never raises IndexError for out-of-range bounds.

### Sorting
- `a.sort()` sorts **in place** and returns `None`.
- `sorted(a)` returns a **new** sorted list and works on any iterable.
- Use `key=` for custom order and `reverse=True` for descending. Sorting is **stable**, so you can sort by several keys in turn.

### Copying
`b = a` makes a second name for the same list. Use `a.copy()`, `a[:]` or `list(a)` for a shallow copy, and `copy.deepcopy` when you have nested mutable objects.

Lists are great for ordered data you modify. For frequent inserts/removals at the front use `collections.deque`; for fast membership tests use a `set`.
keyPoints: Lists are ordered and mutable
Slices return new lists: a[start:stop:step]
sort() is in place and returns None; sorted() returns a new list
key= controls the sort order
b = a does not copy; use a.copy() or a[:]
pitfalls: Assigning the result of a.sort() (it is None)
Removing items while iterating over the same list
Using a list as a default argument

examples.title: Slicing and sorting
examples.code:
nums = [5, 2, 9, 1, 7]
print(nums[0], nums[-1], nums[1:4], nums[::-1], nums[::2])

nums.append(3)
nums.extend([8, 6])
print(nums)
print(sorted(nums))
print(sorted(nums, reverse=True))

words = ["pear", "fig", "banana", "kiwi"]
print(sorted(words, key=len))
print(sorted(words, key=lambda w: (len(w), w)))

people = [("Ana", 30), ("Bo", 25), ("Cy", 30)]
people.sort(key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]))
print(people)

a = [[1], [2]]
b = a.copy()
b[0].append(99)
print(a)   # shallow copy shares inner lists

interview.a: sort() mutates the list in place and returns None; sorted() accepts any iterable and returns a new sorted list.

interview.q: What is the time complexity of list.append and list.insert(0, x)?
interview.a: append is amortised O(1); insert at the front is O(n) because elements shift.
A shallow copy copies the outer list but shares inner objects; a deep copy recursively copies everything.

topics.title: Tuples and Sets
topics.summary: Immutable ordered tuples and unordered collections of unique items called sets.
topics.description:
### Tuples
A `tuple` is an ordered, **immutable** sequence: `point = (3, 4)`. A single-item tuple needs a trailing comma: `(5,)`. Tuples are used for fixed records, as dictionary keys (if all items are hashable) and for returning several values from a function. **Unpacking** is a favourite feature:

```python
x, y = point
first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]
```

Because tuples cannot change, they are slightly faster and safer than lists for constant data.

### Sets
A `set` is an **unordered collection of unique, hashable items**. Create with `{1, 2, 3}` or `set(iterable)` (note `{}` is an empty dict; use `set()` for an empty set).

- Add/remove: `add`, `discard` (no error if missing), `remove` (KeyError if missing).
- Math: `a | b` union, `a & b` intersection, `a - b` difference, `a ^ b` symmetric difference, `a <= b` subset.
- Membership tests are **O(1)** on average, much faster than lists.

### Typical uses
- Remove duplicates: `list(set(items))` (order is lost; use `dict.fromkeys(items)` to keep order).
- Fast "have I seen this?" checks.
- Comparing groups: who is in A but not in B.

`frozenset` is an immutable set that can be used as a dict key or inside another set.
keyPoints: Tuples are immutable and support unpacking
A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma
Sets hold unique hashable items with O(1) membership tests
Use set operators | & - ^ for group maths
set() creates an empty set; {} is a dict
pitfalls: Expecting a set to keep insertion order
Putting a list or dict inside a set (unhashable)

examples.title: Tuples and sets
examples.code:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
first, *rest = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(x, y, first, rest)
single = (5,)
print(type(single), type((5)))

a = {1, 2, 3, 4}
b = {3, 4, 5}
print(a | b, a & b, a - b, a ^ b)
print({1, 2} <= a)

items = ["b", "a", "b", "c", "a"]
print(sorted(set(items)))
print(list(dict.fromkeys(items)))   # unique, order kept

interview.q: Why would you use a tuple instead of a list?
interview.a: For fixed data, as dict keys or set members, and to signal that the data must not change. They are also a bit lighter and faster.

interview.q: How do you remove duplicates while keeping order?
interview.a: list(dict.fromkeys(items)), since dicts preserve insertion order.

topics.title: Dictionaries
topics.summary: Key-value mappings with fast lookups, plus the essential methods and patterns.
topics.description:
A `dict` maps **keys to values** with O(1) average lookup. Since Python 3.7 dictionaries remember insertion order. Keys must be hashable (strings, numbers, tuples of immutables); values can be anything.

### Basics
```python
user = {"name": "Asha", "age": 25}
user["city"] = "Pune"      # add / update
user["name"]               # read (KeyError if missing)
user.get("email", "n/a")   # safe read with default
del user["age"]
```

### Methods you need
`keys()`, `values()`, `items()`, `get()`, `pop()`, `setdefault()`, `update()`, and the merge operator `a | b` (3.9+). Iterate with `for k, v in d.items()`.

### Dict comprehension
`{n: n * n for n in range(5)}` builds a dict in one line.

### Useful patterns
- Counting: `d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1`, or use `collections.Counter`.
- Grouping: `d.setdefault(k, []).append(v)`, or `defaultdict(list)`.
- Inverting: `{v: k for k, v in d.items()}`.
- Nested data: dicts of lists/dicts, exactly the shape of JSON.

### Views
`keys()`, `values()` and `items()` return live **views**, not copies. Convert with `list()` if you need a snapshot, especially before changing the dict while looping.
keyPoints: Keys must be hashable; values can be anything
Use get() or in to avoid KeyError
items() gives (key, value) pairs for loops
Dicts keep insertion order (3.7+)
Dict comprehensions and | merge (3.9+) keep code short
pitfalls: Changing dict size while iterating over it (RuntimeError)
Using a list as a key
Assuming d[k] returns None for missing keys

examples.title: Common dict patterns

interview.a: As hash tables, which gives O(1) average time for get, set and delete. Keys must be hashable.
d[key] raises KeyError when missing; get returns None or a supplied default.
Yes, since Python 3.7 they preserve insertion order as a language guarantee.

topics.title: Comprehensions
topics.summary: Build lists, dicts, sets and generators from iterables in a single readable expression.
topics.description:
A comprehension builds a new collection from an iterable, optionally filtering items. It is shorter and usually faster than the equivalent `for` loop with `append`.

### Forms
```python
[x * 2 for x in nums]                 # list
[x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]       # with filter
{x: x ** 2 for x in nums}             # dict
{len(w) for w in words}               # set
(x * 2 for x in nums)                 # generator expression (lazy)
```

### Conditional expression vs filter
- Filter goes at the end: `[x for x in data if x > 0]`
- Transform with if/else goes at the start: `[x if x > 0 else 0 for x in data]`

### Nested loops
`[(r, c) for r in range(3) for c in range(2)]` reads in the same order as nested `for` statements. Flattening a matrix: `[v for row in m for v in row]`.

### Generator expressions
With round brackets nothing is built up front; values are produced one by one. Use them inside `sum()`, `any()`, `all()`, `max()` to save memory: `sum(x * x for x in range(10**6))`.

### When not to use
If the logic needs several statements, side effects, or deep nesting, write a normal loop. Readability beats cleverness.
keyPoints: [expr for x in it if cond] builds a list
Dict and set comprehensions use {}
Generator expressions use () and are lazy
Filter goes at the end; if/else expression goes in front
Switch to a loop when it stops being readable
pitfalls: Cramming multiple nested conditions into one line
Using a comprehension only for side effects such as print
Keeping a huge list in memory when a generator would do

examples.title: All comprehension types
examples.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
print([n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0])
print([n if n > 3 else 0 for n in nums])
print({n: n % 3 for n in nums})
print({len(w) for w in ["a", "bb", "cc", "ddd"]})

matrix = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
print([v for row in matrix for v in row])
print([[row[i] for row in matrix] for i in range(3)])   # transpose

total = sum(n * n for n in range(1000))
print(total)
print(any(n > 5 for n in nums), all(n > 0 for n in nums))

interview.a: A list comprehension builds the entire list in memory; a generator expression yields items lazily and uses almost no memory.
Usually somewhat, since the loop runs in optimised bytecode without repeated append method lookups, but clarity matters more.

topics.title: collections, heapq and itertools
topics.summary: Specialised containers (Counter, defaultdict, deque, namedtuple), heaps and iterator tools.
topics.description:
The standard library gives you specialised tools that replace a lot of hand-written code.

### collections
- `Counter` counts hashable items: `Counter("hello").most_common(2)`.
- `defaultdict(factory)` creates missing keys automatically: `defaultdict(list)`.
- `deque` is a double-ended queue with O(1) append/pop on both ends; `maxlen` makes a sliding window.
- `namedtuple` gives tuples readable field names: `Point = namedtuple("Point", "x y")`.
- `OrderedDict`, `ChainMap` are less common today.

### heapq
A **min-heap** stored in a plain list. `heappush`, `heappop`, `heapify`, `nlargest(k, it)`, `nsmallest(k, it)`. Use it for priority queues, "top K" and merging sorted streams. Pop always returns the smallest item; for a max-heap push negated values.

### itertools
Lazy iterator building blocks:
`count`, `cycle`, `chain`, `islice`, `zip_longest`, `product` (cartesian), `permutations`, `combinations`, `groupby` (needs sorted input), `accumulate`, `pairwise` (3.10+), `batched` (3.12+).

```python
from itertools import combinations
list(combinations("ABC", 2))   # AB AC BC
```

These functions return iterators, so wrap them in `list()` when you want to see the values and remember an iterator can be consumed only once.
keyPoints: Counter, defaultdict, deque and namedtuple remove boilerplate
deque is O(1) at both ends; list is O(n) at the front
heapq is a min-heap: push, pop, nlargest, nsmallest
itertools returns lazy iterators; groupby needs sorted data
Iterators can be consumed only once
pitfalls: Using list.pop(0) in a queue (O(n)) instead of deque

examples.title: Counter, defaultdict, deque, heapq, itertools
examples.code:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque, namedtuple
import heapq
from itertools import chain, combinations, groupby, islice, product

print(Counter("mississippi").most_common(2))

d = defaultdict(list)
for word in ["ant", "bee", "ape", "bat"]:
    d[word[0]].append(word)
print(dict(d))

q = deque([1, 2, 3], maxlen=3)
q.append(4)
q.appendleft(0)
print(q)

Point = namedtuple("Point", "x y")
p = Point(2, 5)
print(p.x, p.y, p)

h = [7, 2, 9, 4]
heapq.heapify(h)
print(heapq.heappop(h), heapq.nlargest(2, [7, 2, 9, 4]))

print(list(combinations("ABC", 2)))
print(list(product([1, 2], "ab")))
print(list(islice(chain([1, 2], [3, 4]), 3)))
for key, grp in groupby(sorted("aabbbc")):
    print(key, len(list(grp)))

interview.q: When use deque instead of list?
interview.a: When you add or remove at both ends often, such as queues, BFS and sliding windows; deque gives O(1) on both ends.

interview.q: How do you get the k largest items efficiently?
interview.a: heapq.nlargest(k, iterable), O(n log k), or keep a min-heap of size k.
